title: The Ferryman Who Counted Debts
summary: The ferryman of the black river takes no coins — he takes favors, owed and remembered, and he never forgets a debt. When Isla crosses without being able to pay, she becomes bound to him, and learns that a kindness given to be repaid is a chain, while a kindness given freely is the only thing that sets you free.

chapters.title: The Ferryman's Price
chapters.body:
The black river cut the world in two, and the only way across was the ferryman, and the ferryman did not take coins.

He was a tall, grey figure who poled his flat boat across the dark water, and he had ferried travelers over the river for longer than anyone could remember. And his price was strange: he took favors. Not money, not goods — a favor, owed to him, to be called in whenever he chose. You climbed into his boat, and he took you across, and in exchange you owed him a favor, a debt, and he wrote it down in a great black ledger he kept, and he never, ever forgot. Someday, in a week or a year or a lifetime, he would come to you, and call in the favor, and you would have to do whatever he asked, because you owed him, and the ferryman always collected.

Most travelers paid gladly enough. A favor seemed cheap for a crossing. And most of the time, the ferryman's favors were small — carry a message, leave a lantern lit, plant a particular flower on a particular grave. But the wise among the river-folk warned their children: be careful crossing with the ferryman. A debt to him is a chain, and he holds the other end, and you never know when he'll pull it, or what he'll ask, or how long you'll be bound. Owe him too much, they said, and you belong to him. And there were tales of travelers so deep in debt to the ferryman — crossing again and again, favor upon favor — that they'd become his, bound to serve him forever, poling the boat beside him in the grey, working off debts that only ever grew.

Isla was thirteen, and she needed to cross the black river to reach a healer on the far side, for her little brother was sick and the only cure grew across the water. She had no coins that would have mattered anyway, and no favor she felt she could safely promise — she was only a child, with nothing to offer. But her brother was sick, and the healer was across the river, and the ferryman was the only way.

So Isla climbed into the flat boat, and the ferryman poled her across the black water, and on the far side he opened his great ledger and looked at her with eyes like cold river-stones.

"A favor," he said. "That is the price. Owed to me, to be called in when I choose. What do you offer, child?"

And Isla, who had nothing, and who was frightened, and who needed to get to the healer and back, said the thing that trapped her: "I don't have anything. But I'll owe you. Whatever you want. Please — I just need to get the cure for my brother. I'll owe you a favor. Anything."

The ferryman's stone eyes glinted, and he wrote in his ledger — Isla, one favor, and then, after a pause, a second line — and one favor for the crossing back — and he closed the book.

"Anything," he repeated softly. "That is a large word, child, to a ferryman who counts debts. You have promised me anything, twice over. Go and get your cure. I will collect when I choose. And remember — I never forget a debt."

chapters.title: The Debt That Grew
chapters.body:
Isla got the cure, and her brother recovered, and for a while she almost forgot the debt. But the ferryman did not forget. The ferryman never forgot.

He came for her first favor within the month. He appeared at the edge of the village one evening, grey and tall, and called in her debt: he needed her to carry a heavy message-stone to a village three days' walk away. It was hard, and it was frightening for a girl alone, but she owed him, so she did it. And when she returned, exhausted, she found he'd already noted her second debt — the crossing back she'd promised — and called that in too: another task, harder than the first. And when she'd done that one, somehow there was another. Because here was the trap Isla slowly began to understand: the ferryman's favors were designed to create new debts. He'd send her on a task that required crossing the river again — and crossing meant a new favor owed — so that every debt she paid off spawned another, and the ledger never emptied, only grew.

Isla found herself bound to the ferryman, working off debts that multiplied faster than she could pay them, her life no longer her own. She was always in his service, always owing, always waiting for the next time he'd appear to call in a favor. She'd promised him anything, twice, out of desperation, and he had turned that anything into an endless chain, and she was becoming — she could feel it — one of those travelers the river-folk warned about, so deep in debt to the ferryman that she belonged to him.

One grey evening, poling a borrowed boat back across the river on yet another of his errands, Isla met another of the ferryman's debtors — an old man, grey-faced and tired, working alongside the ferryman in the mist, and she realized with horror that he had once been a traveler like her, bound so long ago and so deeply that he'd become part of the ferry itself, poling the boat forever, his debt grown beyond any hope of paying. And the old man looked at Isla with pity and warned her, in a whisper, "Don't try to pay him off, child. That's the trap. Every debt you pay creates another. You can't buy your way free of the ferryman. The more you give him to settle your debt, the more you owe. I've been paying for forty years, and I owe more now than when I started."

"Then how do I get free?" Isla whispered back, desperate.

The old man was quiet for a moment, and then he said something strange. "I don't know. I never found the way. But I'll tell you what I've come to think, in forty years of poling this boat. The ferryman deals in debts — in favors given so they can be collected, kindnesses that are really just loans. And a debt is a chain; that's its nature; you can't make a chain into freedom by adding more links. I think the only thing that isn't a chain — the only thing the ferryman can't hold the other end of — is a kindness given freely. Given for nothing. Given with no debt attached, expecting nothing back. But I never had the courage or the wit to test it. Maybe you will."

And Isla, poling through the grey mist, bound in an ever-growing chain of debts, turned the old man's words over and over, and began to understand what he might mean — and what it might cost her to try it.

chapters.title: The Kindness Freely Given
chapters.body:
The next time the ferryman came to call in a favor, Isla was ready — not with a payment, but with an idea that frightened her, because it meant doing the opposite of everything the ferryman's world ran on.

He appeared, grey and tall, and opened his ledger to add another task to her endless debt. But before he could speak, Isla did something no debtor had ever done. She said: "Wait. Before you tell me what I owe — I want to do something for you. Freely. Not to pay a debt. Not because I owe you. Just because." And she looked at the ferryman — really looked at him, this cold grey figure who had poled the black river alone for longer than anyone could remember, collecting debts, holding chains, and who had, she suddenly saw, no one who had ever done a single thing for him without being forced to by a debt. "You've been alone out here forever," Isla said softly. "Poling this river, keeping your ledger, and everyone who crosses only ever gives you things because they owe you. No one's ever just... been kind to you. For nothing. Have they?"

The ferryman went very still.

And Isla gave him a kindness, freely. She had brought with her a warm loaf of bread and a small lantern — and she gave them to him, not as payment, not entered in any ledger, expecting nothing back. "This is for you," she said. "Because it's cold out here, and dark, and you've been alone a long time. You don't owe me anything for it. It's not a favor. It's just a gift. Freely given."

And something happened to the ferryman that had not happened in all his long years. The cold river-stone eyes changed. Something old and frozen in him seemed to crack, just slightly, and warm. Because he dealt only in debts — in kindnesses that were loans, favors that were chains — and he had forgotten, if he had ever known, that a kindness could be given for nothing, freely, expecting no return. It astonished him. It reached a part of him that no debt ever could, because a debt binds, but a free gift simply... warms. And you cannot collect on a free gift. You cannot hold the other end of a chain that was never a chain. There was nothing to write in the ledger, because Isla had given him something that existed entirely outside the whole system of owing and collecting that was the only world he knew.

"Why?" the ferryman asked, and his voice was different — softer, almost bewildered. "You owe me. You could have tried to pay. Why give me something for nothing, when you're already so deep in debt?"

"Because a debt is a chain," Isla said, "and you can't make a chain into freedom by adding links. I've been trying to pay you off for months, and every payment only bound me tighter. So I stopped trying to pay. I gave you something free instead. Because I think — I think free kindness is the only thing in the world that isn't a chain. And I'd rather give you that than owe you forever."

And the ferryman looked at her for a long, long moment, and then he did something he had never done in all his years of counting debts. He opened his great black ledger, and he found the pages with Isla's name, and all her multiplying debts — and he closed the book, and he set it aside, and he said: "Your debts are cleared. All of them." He looked at her with eyes that were no longer cold. "Not because you paid them. You can't pay them; that was always the trap, and you're the first to see it. Your debts are cleared because you gave me something no debt could ever buy, and no ledger could ever hold. You were kind to me. Freely. For nothing. And a free kindness, child — I had forgotten — cannot be owed, and cannot be collected, and cannot be a chain. It can only be given, and received, and it sets both people free. You've set me free of collecting from you. And in doing it, you've set yourself free of owing."

And Isla was free. The chain of debts simply dissolved, because it had been undone by the one thing that isn't a debt.

But the story did not quite end there. Because the old man — the one who'd been poling the boat for forty years, bound by debts grown beyond all paying — had watched the whole thing from the mist. And Isla turned to him, and understood that she could do for him what she'd done for the ferryman, and what he'd been too tired and trapped to do for himself. She went to the old man, and she gave him a free kindness too — helped him, freely, for nothing, expecting no return — and she showed the ferryman, whose frozen heart had cracked open, that the old man's endless debt could be cleared the same way hers had been: not paid, but dissolved, by kindness freely given and freely received. And the ferryman, changed now, cleared the old man's debt as well, and the old man wept, forty years of chains falling away, and walked free at last across the black river he'd been bound to for a lifetime.

The ferryman still ferries travelers across the black river. But something changed in him after Isla, and the river-folk began to notice it. He still takes a favor for a crossing, for that is his way — but he no longer designs his favors to multiply, no longer traps his debtors in growing chains, no longer holds anyone forever. And now and then, when a traveler crosses who has nothing to offer, and is frightened, and is only trying to help someone they love — the ferryman has been known to pole them across for nothing at all. A free kindness, given for its own sake, expecting no return. Because Isla taught him the thing he'd forgotten in all his long grey years: that a kindness given to be repaid is a loan, and a loan is a chain, and chains only ever grow heavier. But a kindness given freely, for nothing, is the only thing in all the world that sets both the giver and the receiver free.
